title: Kant and duty
examples: What exactly does Kant mean by 'duty' in ethics?
How is the categorical imperative different from just following rules?
Can you give another example of treating people as ends?

explain.say: Kant believed that morality comes from duty, not from feelings.
The categorical imperative is a universal moral test for actions.
One test is the universal law formulation, testing consistency.
Another test is the humanity formulation, respecting rational beings always.

items: Do not use people merely as means

explain.say: For example, promising to keep a secret shows respect for trust.
In real life, voting for a law shows duty to the community.

faq.q: What is the difference between acting from duty and acting from sympathy?
faq.a: Acting from duty means you follow a moral rule because it is right, regardless of how you feel. You might also act from sympathy, which means you help someone because you feel bad for them. You might ask: Why is feeling good not enough for morality? Or, how does Kant separate feeling from duty?
asks: Is sympathy enough for moral action?
What is the difference between duty and feeling?

faq.q: Can the categorical imperative ever be broken?
faq.a: Kant suggests that if an action violates a universal moral law, it is morally wrong. However, he acknowledges situations where duties conflict, which is complex. You might also ask: Are there exceptions to the rules? Or, what if two duties clash?

faq.q: What does it mean to treat someone as an end?
faq.a: It means recognizing that the person has inherent worth and should never only be used to achieve your own goals. You must respect their ability to make their own choices. You might ask: Is using someone for money okay? Or, what is inherent worth?
asks: Can I use someone if it helps me?

faq.q: Is this system too strict for real life?
faq.a: Some critics find it too rigid because it demands adherence to rules even when outcomes might be better. Kantian ethics emphasizes the moral quality of the will itself. You might also ask: Does this ignore consequences? Or, is it too demanding?

faq.q: Does Kant care about the outcome of an action?
faq.a: No, Kantian ethics focuses on the motive or the will behind the action, not the result. The moral worth comes from acting out of respect for the moral law. You might also ask: Does the result matter at all? Or, is the motive everything?
asks: What is the focus: motive or result?

facts: Kant argued that moral laws must be universal.
The categorical imperative tests maxims for universal consistency.
Treating people as ends means respecting their rationality.
Moral worth comes from acting out of duty, not feeling.

quiz.say: If you help a friend because you expect them to help you later, are you acting from duty?
quiz.why: You are acting from inclination because you expect a return benefit.

wrong.0: This mistake incorrectly links duty to direct request.
wrong.2: This mistake confuses expected outcomes with moral obligation.
wrong.3: This mistake focuses only on the positive outcome, ignoring the motive.

quiz.say: Which formulation requires testing if a rule can apply to everyone always?
quiz.why: This formulation directly tests the universal applicability of your rule.

wrong.0: This formulation focuses on the worth of people, not the rule itself.
wrong.1: This is too general; the specific test name is required.
wrong.2: This describes the concept, but not the specific formal test.

quiz.say: If you use a person only to get a grade, which principle are you violating?

options.show: It is not a moral violation
options.say: It is not a moral violation

quiz.why: This violates the principle that people must be treated as ends in themselves.

wrong.0: This describes the motive, not the specific moral principle violated.
wrong.1: This wrongly dismisses the inherent moral weight of the action.
wrong.3: While it is wrong, the specific violation is about personhood.
